newsitem.title: USA: Senate wants all countries in climate change deal.
newsitem.headline: Senate wants all countries in climate change deal.

text.p: The U.S. Senate on Friday warned the Clinton administration to reject a global warming treaty unless it forces developing countries to join industrialised nations in fighting heat-trapping pollution.
The resolution, which also said the U.S. should reject a treaty that harms its economy, passed 95-0.

The White House would need Senate confirmation of the treaty it is negotiating with other industrialised countries to reduce pollution from burning fossil fuels that is blamed for warming the atmosphere.

"This resolution rejects the United Nations' current negotiating strategy of binding the United States and other developed nations to legally-binding reductions without requiring any new or binding commitments from 130 nations such as China, Mexico, and South Korea," Nebraska Republican Chuck Hagel, a co-sponsor of the measure, said.

The so-called Berlin Mandate, agreed to by the United States and other industrialised countries, calls on them to commit to meeting targets to reduce pollution on the grounds that they are responsible for almost all the existing build-up of carbon gases. But developing countries would not face binding limits.

"Unfortunately, a fundamental error -- I would use the word blunder -- was made in Berlin, in that only the so-called developed nations ... were to impose a legally binding regime on themselves. Developing nations got a free pass," West Virginia Democrat Robert Byrd, the measure's other main sponsor, said.

"I do not think the Senate should support a treaty that requires only half the world, i.e. the developed countries, to endure the economic costs of reducing emissions, while developing countries are free to pollute the atmosphere, and, in so doing, siphon off American industries," added Byrd, whose coal-producing state could be hit hard by pollution controls.

The resolution drew support from senators who dispute whether global warming is a real threat and oppose a treaty, to those who said prompt action is needed to slow climate changes that already are apparent.

"I have joined in the notion that it is appropriate to reconsider the Berlin mandate," Massachusetts Democrat John Kerry, who led forces stressing the need to fight climate change, said. "This is about how we will approach the problem of greenhouse gases, not whether."

But several other senators said they felt the Clinton administration was using scare tactics of potentially dire consequences of climate change -- rising sea levels, more intense storms, spreading tropical diseases -- to muster support for a treaty.
"The president and the vice president stand next to flooded homes in North Dakota and suggest this is a result of global warming. That's not fair," Idaho Republican Larry Craig said.
The U.S. position is to call on developing countries that have significant emissions to agree to negotiate binding pollution limits that they would adopt by 2005.
But Byrd said: "A promise from developing countries to only negotiate at a later date is simply unacceptable."
